title: A barrier two layers thick
question: How can a membrane only nanometers thick keep a cell's contents in?
hook: Cells are wrapped in a film made of molecules that sort themselves around water.
idea: Phospholipids self-assemble in water into two layers with tails inward, forming a thin barrier that blocks most water-soluble molecules.

beats.prompt: A sugar dissolved in water reaches the center of a bilayer. What happens to the sugar?

choices.label: It dissolves freely and passes straight through
choices.feedback: The center holds almost no water, so water-soluble sugars have nothing to dissolve in.

choices.label: It is excluded from the center
It collects there and tears the bilayer apart
choices.feedback: The center simply excludes sugars; nothing says they break the bilayer.

beats.explain: The center of a bilayer contains almost no water and excludes molecules like sugars or salts that dissolve in water.

beats.prompt: Match each region of the bilayer to its description.
beats.explain: Moving in from the water, the bilayer has a hydrated headgroup, a partly hydrated boundary layer and a hydrophobic core.

beats.prompt: Is each part of a phospholipid hydrophilic or hydrophobic?
items: Part pointing toward the center of the sheet
beats.explain: The phosphate head is hydrophilic and the two fatty acid chain tails are hydrophobic, so the tails point toward the center.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Phospholipids have a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.
In water they self-assemble into two layers, with the tails toward the center.
So the center of the bilayer is full of water, letting salts and sugars dissolve through.
Therefore ions cross only when ion pumps move them across.
beats.explain: The center contains almost no water and excludes molecules that dissolve in water.
